scope: Read-only verification of committed content and local native/serving bytes. This report does not assert deployment, final public preview URLs, live downloads, or private archive readback. Publication URL bindings and release documentation may be updated separately by the release owner.

physical_scale.policy: Catalogue dimensions are descriptive. Unverified display scale, support geometry and original-versus-replica uncertainty do not imply physical calibration.

qualifications_verified: Historical casts and replicas retain explicit identity, material and date qualifications.
All 18 SMK casts identify plaster; documented cast dimensions are not silently replaced by original-object dimensions.
Both Japanese figurines label dimensions as underlying originals and retain uncertainty about the photographed 2019 museum display.
Shigir remains a physical head fragment with no whole-idol dimension assigned.

Architectural installations and partial/unrecorded surfaces retain the reviewed source qualifications.

deduplication.manual_composition_review: The independent pre-release metadata audit checked translated title aliases, artists, accessions and composition against all2180 baseline records; no confirmed composition repeats. Distinct preparatory studies and explicitly identified historical representations were retained as reviewed.

exhibition_placements.caption: Narmer appears at a commanding scale on both sides of this ceremonial palette. Crowns, attendants and defeated figures turn the ruler’s body into an image of authority. Rotate the object to compare its two carved faces.
A royal encounter occupies the top of a tall field of writing. The carved image and the inscribed laws give Hammurabi’s authority both a visible form and a durable material presence.

Donatello places the Annunciation inside an elaborate architectural frame. The figures’ gestures bring an intimate exchange into the public setting of Santa Croce; the surrounding wall remains part of this in-place recording.

The child wraps his arms around the goose as their bodies press in opposite directions. This Roman marble after a Greek composition makes a small struggle into a balanced group, inviting comparison from the sides and back.

This surviving head fragment belongs to the Great Shigir Idol, carved from larch in the early Mesolithic. Its open mouth, incised face and broken neck remain legible in the museum’s separate model of the head. The untextured model records form without recreating the wood’s surface color.

A damaged ancient group acquired another life as one of Rome’s talking statues. The surviving bodies now stand on a street pedestal associated with anonymous satire. Both ancient losses and the later urban setting shape how the work is encountered.

A blue hippopotamus carries painted river plants across its body. The animal’s rounded form and small scale belong to a Middle Kingdom funerary object; three of its legs are museum restorations, retained in this recording.

Jewelry and carefully modeled features distinguish this bronze cat. The seated pose combines an observed animal with the ceremonial presence of an Egyptian sacred image. Turn the model to follow its tail and the shape of its back.
